# Fermat pseudoprime

- [العربية](https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D8%A3%D8%B9%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AF_%D9%81%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%85%D8%A7_%D8%B4%D8%A8%D9%87_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9)
- [Deutsch](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermatsche_Pseudoprimzahl)
- [Español](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%BAmero_pseudoprimo_de_Fermat)
- [Polski](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liczby_pseudopierwsze_Fermata)
- [Русский](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9F%D1%81%D0%B5%D0%B2%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%82%D1%8B%D0%B5_%D1%87%D0%B8%D1%81%D0%BB%D0%B0_%D0%A4%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BC%D0%B0)
- [Svenska](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermatpseudoprimtal)
- [中文](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B4%B9%E9%A9%AC%E4%BC%AA%E7%B4%A0%E6%95%B0)
 [Edit links](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityPage/Q1406394#sitelinks-wikipedia)                          From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia   Composite number that passes Fermat's probable primality test

In [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory), the **Fermat pseudoprimes** make up the most important class of [pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoprime) that come from [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem).

## Definition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=1)]

[Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem) states that if     p   {\displaystyle p}   is prime and     a   {\displaystyle a}   is [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime) to     p   {\displaystyle p}  , then      a  p − 1   − 1   {\displaystyle a^{p-1}-1}   is [divisible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor) by     p   {\displaystyle p}  . For a positive integer     a   {\displaystyle a}  , if a composite integer     x   {\displaystyle x}   divides      a  x − 1   − 1   {\displaystyle a^{x-1}-1}   then     x   {\displaystyle x}   is called a **Fermat pseudoprime** to base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-JoyOfFactoring-1): Def. 3.32

In other words, a composite integer is a Fermat pseudoprime to base     a   {\displaystyle a}   if it successfully passes the [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test) for the base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-desmedt-10-23-2) The false statement that all numbers that pass the Fermat primality test for base 2 are prime is called the [Chinese hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_hypothesis).

The smallest base-2 Fermat pseudoprime is 341. It is not a prime, since it equals 11·31, but it satisfies Fermat's little theorem:      2  340   ≡ 1 (  mod  341   )   {\displaystyle 2^{340}\equiv 1({\bmod {341}})}   and thus passes the [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test) for the base 2.

Pseudoprimes to base 2 are sometimes called **Sarrus numbers**, after [P. F. Sarrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Sarrus) who discovered that 341 has this property, **Poulet numbers**, after [P. Poulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Poulet) who made a table of such numbers, or **Fermatians** (sequence [A001567](https://oeis.org/A001567) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences)).

A Fermat pseudoprime is often called a **pseudoprime**, with the modifier **Fermat** being understood.

An integer     x   {\displaystyle x}   that is a Fermat pseudoprime for all values of     a   {\displaystyle a}   that are coprime to     x   {\displaystyle x}   is called a [Carmichael number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-desmedt-10-23-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-JoyOfFactoring-1): Def. 3.34

## Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=2)]

### Distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=3)]

There are infinitely many pseudoprimes to any given base     a > 1   {\displaystyle a>1}  . In 1904, Cipolla showed how to produce an infinite number of pseudoprimes to base     a > 1   {\displaystyle a>1}  : let     A = (  a  p   − 1 )  /  ( a − 1 )   {\displaystyle A=(a^{p}-1)/(a-1)}   and let     B = (  a  p   + 1 )  /  ( a + 1 )   {\displaystyle B=(a^{p}+1)/(a+1)}  , where     p   {\displaystyle p}   is a prime number that does not divide     a (  a  2   − 1 )   {\displaystyle a(a^{2}-1)}  . Then     n = A B   {\displaystyle n=AB}   is composite, and is a pseudoprime to base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-4) For example, if     a = 2   {\displaystyle a=2}   and     p = 5   {\displaystyle p=5}  , then     A = 31   {\displaystyle A=31}  ,     B = 11   {\displaystyle B=11}  , and     n = A B = 341   {\displaystyle n=AB=341}   is a pseudoprime to base     2   {\displaystyle 2}  .

In fact, there are infinitely many [strong pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) to any base greater than 1 (see Theorem 1 of [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-PSW-5)) and infinitely many Carmichael numbers,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-Alford1994-6) but they are comparatively rare. There are three pseudoprimes to base 2 below 1000, 245 below one million, and 21853 less than 25·109. There are 4842 strong pseudoprimes base 2 and 2163 Carmichael numbers below this limit (see Table 1 of [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-PSW-5)).

Starting at 17·257, the product of consecutive Fermat numbers is a base-2 pseudoprime, and so are all [Fermat composites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_prime) and [Mersenne composites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_prime).

The probability of a composite number n passing the Fermat test approaches zero for     n → ∞   {\displaystyle n\to \infty }  . Specifically, Kim and Pomerance showed the following: The probability that a random odd number     n ≤ x   {\displaystyle n\leq x}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to a random base     1 < b < n − 1   {\displaystyle 1<b<n-1}   is less than 2.77·10−8 for x= 10100, and is at most (log x)−197<10−10,000 for x≥10100,000.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-7) For a fixed base b, the proportion of pseudoprimes up to x is at most e-log x log log log x/(2 log log x) for large x.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-8)

## Bases *b* for which *n* is a Fermat pseudoprime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=7)]

If composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is even, then     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to the trivial base     b ≡ 1   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b\equiv 1{\pmod {n}}}  . If composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is odd, then     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to the trivial bases     b ≡ ± 1   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b\equiv \pm 1{\pmod {n}}}  .

For any composite     n   {\displaystyle n}  , the *number* of distinct bases     b   {\displaystyle b}   modulo     n   {\displaystyle n}  , for which     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime base     b   {\displaystyle b}  , is [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-10): Thm. 1, p. 1392

      ∏  i = 1   k   gcd (  p  i   − 1 , n − 1 )   {\displaystyle \prod _{i=1}^{k}\gcd(p_{i}-1,n-1)}

where      p  1   , … ,  p  k     {\displaystyle p_{1},\dots ,p_{k}}   are the distinct prime factors of     n   {\displaystyle n}  . This includes the trivial bases.

For example, for     n = 341 = 11 ⋅ 31   {\displaystyle n=341=11\cdot 31}  , this product is     gcd ( 10 , 340 ) ⋅ gcd ( 30 , 340 ) = 100   {\displaystyle \gcd(10,340)\cdot \gcd(30,340)=100}  . For     n = 341   {\displaystyle n=341}  , the smallest such nontrivial base is     b = 2   {\displaystyle b=2}  .

Every odd composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to at least two nontrivial bases modulo     n   {\displaystyle n}   unless     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a power of 3.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-10): Cor. 1, p. 1393

## Weak pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=8)]

A composite number *n* which satisfies      b  n   ≡ b   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b^{n}\equiv b{\pmod {n}}}   is called a **weak pseudoprime to base *b***. For any given base *b*, all Fermat pseudoprimes are weak pseudoprimes, and all weak pseudoprimes coprime to *b* are Fermat pseudoprimes. However, this definition also permits some pseudoprimes which are *not* coprime to *b*.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-11) For example, the smallest even weak pseudoprime to base 2 is 161038 (see (sequence [A006935](https://oeis.org/A006935) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))).

The least weak pseudoprime to bases *b* = 1, 2, ... are:

 4, 341, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 4, 4, 14, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 22, 4, 4, 9, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 9, 4, 4, 38, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 46, 4, 4, 10, ... [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences): [A000790](https://oeis.org/A000790)

This sequence is [periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_sequence) with period 277#×23#, where # is the [primorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primorial).

The least weak pseudoprime is called the **primary pretender**[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-12).

[Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number) are weak pseudoprimes to all bases, thus all terms in this list are less than or equal to the smallest Carmichael number, 561. Except for 561 = 3⋅11⋅17, only [semiprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiprime) can occur in the above sequence. Not all semiprimes less than 561 occur; a semiprime *pq* (*p* ≤ *q*) less than 561 occurs in the above sequences [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) *p* − 1 divides *q* − 1 (see (sequence [A108574](https://oeis.org/A108574) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))). The least Fermat pseudoprime to base *b* (also not necessary exceeding *b*) ((sequence [A090086](https://oeis.org/A090086) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))) is *usually* semiprime, but not always; the first counterexample is [A090086](https://oeis.org/A090086)(648) = 385 = 5 × 7 × 11.

If we require *n* > *b*, the least weak pseudoprimes (for *b* = 1, 2, ...) are:

 4, 341, 6, 6, 10, 10, 14, 9, 12, 15, 15, 22, 21, 15, 21, 20, 34, 25, 38, 21, 28, 33, 33, 25, 28, 27, 39, 36, 35, 49, 49, 33, 44, 35, 45, 42, 45, 39, 57, 52, 82, 66, 77, 45, 55, 69, 65, 49, 56, 51, ... [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences): [A239293](https://oeis.org/A239293)

## Euler pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=9)] Main article: [Euler pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_pseudoprime)

Euler pseudoprimes are a subset of the Fermat pseudoprimes for any given base     a   {\displaystyle a}  . There also exists absolute Euler pseudoprimes, which are a subset of the [Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number), and which are the analogue of Carmichael numbers for Euler pseudoprimes.

## Euler–Jacobi pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=10)] Main article: [Euler–Jacobi pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Jacobi_pseudoprime)

Another approach is to use more refined notions of pseudoprimality, e.g. [strong pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) or [Euler–Jacobi pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Jacobi_pseudoprime), for which there are no analogues of [Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number). This leads to [probabilistic algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_algorithm) such as the [Solovay–Strassen primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay%E2%80%93Strassen_primality_test), the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test), and the [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test), which produce what are known as [industrial-grade primes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial-grade_primes). Industrial-grade primes are integers for which primality has not been "certified" (i.e. rigorously proven), but have undergone a test such as the Miller–Rabin test which has nonzero, but arbitrarily low, probability of failure.

## Deceptive nonprime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=11)]

A **deceptive nonprime** (called **deceptive prime** by Francis and Ray) is a composite numbers *k* that divide the [repunit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit) with length *k*−1[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-13), a composite number is a deceptive nonprime if and only if it is a Fermat pseudoprime to base 10 and not divisible by 3, the deceptive nonprimes are

 91, 259, 451, 481, 703, 1729, 2821, 2981, 3367, 4141, 4187, 5461, 6533, 6541, 6601, 7471, 7777, 8149, 8401, 8911, 10001, 11111, 12403, 13981, 14701, 14911, 15211, 15841, 19201, ... (sequence [A000864](https://oeis.org/A000864) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

A related sequence is **repunit pseudoprime**, defined as a composite number *k* such that the repunit with length *k* is congruent to 1 mod *k*, a composite number is a repunit pseudoprime if and only if it is a weak pseudoprime to base 10 and not divisible by 3, the repunit pseudoprimes are

 10, 55, 91, 259, 370, 385, 451, 481, 505, 703, 715, 1045, 1105, 1729, 2035, 2465, 2821, 2981, 3367, 4141, 4187, 5005, 5461, 6533, 6541, 6565, 6601, 7471, 7777, 8149, 8401, 8695, 8905, 8911, ... (sequence [A303608](https://oeis.org/A303608) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

## Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=12)]

The rarity of such pseudoprimes has important practical implications. For example, [public-key cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptography) algorithms such as [RSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(algorithm)) require the ability to quickly find large primes. The usual algorithm to generate prime numbers is to generate random odd numbers and [test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primality_test) them for primality. However, [deterministic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterministic_algorithm) primality tests are slow. If the user is willing to tolerate an arbitrarily small chance that the number found is not a prime number but a pseudoprime, it is possible to use the much faster and simpler [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test).

In [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory), the **Fermat pseudoprimes** make up the most important class of [pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoprime) that come from [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem).

Definition

# Definition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=1)]

[Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat's_little_theorem) states that if     p   {\displaystyle p}   is prime and     a   {\displaystyle a}   is [coprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprime) to     p   {\displaystyle p}  , then      a  p − 1   − 1   {\displaystyle a^{p-1}-1}   is [divisible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor) by     p   {\displaystyle p}  . For a positive integer     a   {\displaystyle a}  , if a composite integer     x   {\displaystyle x}   divides      a  x − 1   − 1   {\displaystyle a^{x-1}-1}   then     x   {\displaystyle x}   is called a **Fermat pseudoprime** to base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-JoyOfFactoring-1): Def. 3.32

In other words, a composite integer is a Fermat pseudoprime to base     a   {\displaystyle a}   if it successfully passes the [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test) for the base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-desmedt-10-23-2) The false statement that all numbers that pass the Fermat primality test for base 2 are prime is called the [Chinese hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_hypothesis).

The smallest base-2 Fermat pseudoprime is 341. It is not a prime, since it equals 11·31, but it satisfies Fermat's little theorem:      2  340   ≡ 1 (  mod  341   )   {\displaystyle 2^{340}\equiv 1({\bmod {341}})}   and thus passes the [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test) for the base 2.

Pseudoprimes to base 2 are sometimes called **Sarrus numbers**, after [P. F. Sarrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Sarrus) who discovered that 341 has this property, **Poulet numbers**, after [P. Poulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Poulet) who made a table of such numbers, or **Fermatians** (sequence [A001567](https://oeis.org/A001567) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences)).

A Fermat pseudoprime is often called a **pseudoprime**, with the modifier **Fermat** being understood.

An integer     x   {\displaystyle x}   that is a Fermat pseudoprime for all values of     a   {\displaystyle a}   that are coprime to     x   {\displaystyle x}   is called a [Carmichael number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-desmedt-10-23-2)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-JoyOfFactoring-1): Def. 3.34

Properties

# Properties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=2)]

Distribution

# Distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=3)]

There are infinitely many pseudoprimes to any given base     a > 1   {\displaystyle a>1}  . In 1904, Cipolla showed how to produce an infinite number of pseudoprimes to base     a > 1   {\displaystyle a>1}  : let     A = (  a  p   − 1 )  /  ( a − 1 )   {\displaystyle A=(a^{p}-1)/(a-1)}   and let     B = (  a  p   + 1 )  /  ( a + 1 )   {\displaystyle B=(a^{p}+1)/(a+1)}  , where     p   {\displaystyle p}   is a prime number that does not divide     a (  a  2   − 1 )   {\displaystyle a(a^{2}-1)}  . Then     n = A B   {\displaystyle n=AB}   is composite, and is a pseudoprime to base     a   {\displaystyle a}  .[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-4) For example, if     a = 2   {\displaystyle a=2}   and     p = 5   {\displaystyle p=5}  , then     A = 31   {\displaystyle A=31}  ,     B = 11   {\displaystyle B=11}  , and     n = A B = 341   {\displaystyle n=AB=341}   is a pseudoprime to base     2   {\displaystyle 2}  .

In fact, there are infinitely many [strong pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) to any base greater than 1 (see Theorem 1 of [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-PSW-5)) and infinitely many Carmichael numbers,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-Alford1994-6) but they are comparatively rare. There are three pseudoprimes to base 2 below 1000, 245 below one million, and 21853 less than 25·109. There are 4842 strong pseudoprimes base 2 and 2163 Carmichael numbers below this limit (see Table 1 of [[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-PSW-5)).

Starting at 17·257, the product of consecutive Fermat numbers is a base-2 pseudoprime, and so are all [Fermat composites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_prime) and [Mersenne composites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_prime).

The probability of a composite number n passing the Fermat test approaches zero for     n → ∞   {\displaystyle n\to \infty }  . Specifically, Kim and Pomerance showed the following: The probability that a random odd number     n ≤ x   {\displaystyle n\leq x}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to a random base     1 < b < n − 1   {\displaystyle 1<b<n-1}   is less than 2.77·10−8 for x= 10100, and is at most (log x)−197<10−10,000 for x≥10100,000.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-7) For a fixed base b, the proportion of pseudoprimes up to x is at most e-log x log log log x/(2 log log x) for large x.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-8)

Bases *b* for which *n* is a Fermat pseudoprime

# Bases *b* for which *n* is a Fermat pseudoprime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=7)]

If composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is even, then     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to the trivial base     b ≡ 1   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b\equiv 1{\pmod {n}}}  . If composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is odd, then     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to the trivial bases     b ≡ ± 1   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b\equiv \pm 1{\pmod {n}}}  .

For any composite     n   {\displaystyle n}  , the *number* of distinct bases     b   {\displaystyle b}   modulo     n   {\displaystyle n}  , for which     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime base     b   {\displaystyle b}  , is [[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-10): Thm. 1, p. 1392

      ∏  i = 1   k   gcd (  p  i   − 1 , n − 1 )   {\displaystyle \prod _{i=1}^{k}\gcd(p_{i}-1,n-1)}

where      p  1   , … ,  p  k     {\displaystyle p_{1},\dots ,p_{k}}   are the distinct prime factors of     n   {\displaystyle n}  . This includes the trivial bases.

For example, for     n = 341 = 11 ⋅ 31   {\displaystyle n=341=11\cdot 31}  , this product is     gcd ( 10 , 340 ) ⋅ gcd ( 30 , 340 ) = 100   {\displaystyle \gcd(10,340)\cdot \gcd(30,340)=100}  . For     n = 341   {\displaystyle n=341}  , the smallest such nontrivial base is     b = 2   {\displaystyle b=2}  .

Every odd composite     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a Fermat pseudoprime to at least two nontrivial bases modulo     n   {\displaystyle n}   unless     n   {\displaystyle n}   is a power of 3.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-lpsp-10): Cor. 1, p. 1393

Weak pseudoprimes

# Weak pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=8)]

A composite number *n* which satisfies      b  n   ≡ b   ( mod  n )    {\displaystyle b^{n}\equiv b{\pmod {n}}}   is called a **weak pseudoprime to base *b***. For any given base *b*, all Fermat pseudoprimes are weak pseudoprimes, and all weak pseudoprimes coprime to *b* are Fermat pseudoprimes. However, this definition also permits some pseudoprimes which are *not* coprime to *b*.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-11) For example, the smallest even weak pseudoprime to base 2 is 161038 (see (sequence [A006935](https://oeis.org/A006935) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))).

The least weak pseudoprime to bases *b* = 1, 2, ... are:

 4, 341, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 4, 4, 14, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 22, 4, 4, 9, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 9, 4, 4, 38, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 46, 4, 4, 10, ... [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences): [A000790](https://oeis.org/A000790)

This sequence is [periodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_sequence) with period 277#×23#, where # is the [primorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primorial).

The least weak pseudoprime is called the **primary pretender**[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-12).

[Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number) are weak pseudoprimes to all bases, thus all terms in this list are less than or equal to the smallest Carmichael number, 561. Except for 561 = 3⋅11⋅17, only [semiprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiprime) can occur in the above sequence. Not all semiprimes less than 561 occur; a semiprime *pq* (*p* ≤ *q*) less than 561 occurs in the above sequences [if and only if](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_and_only_if) *p* − 1 divides *q* − 1 (see (sequence [A108574](https://oeis.org/A108574) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))). The least Fermat pseudoprime to base *b* (also not necessary exceeding *b*) ((sequence [A090086](https://oeis.org/A090086) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))) is *usually* semiprime, but not always; the first counterexample is [A090086](https://oeis.org/A090086)(648) = 385 = 5 × 7 × 11.

If we require *n* > *b*, the least weak pseudoprimes (for *b* = 1, 2, ...) are:

 4, 341, 6, 6, 10, 10, 14, 9, 12, 15, 15, 22, 21, 15, 21, 20, 34, 25, 38, 21, 28, 33, 33, 25, 28, 27, 39, 36, 35, 49, 49, 33, 44, 35, 45, 42, 45, 39, 57, 52, 82, 66, 77, 45, 55, 69, 65, 49, 56, 51, ... [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences): [A239293](https://oeis.org/A239293)

Euler pseudoprimes

# Euler pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=9)] Main article: [Euler pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_pseudoprime)

Euler pseudoprimes are a subset of the Fermat pseudoprimes for any given base     a   {\displaystyle a}  . There also exists absolute Euler pseudoprimes, which are a subset of the [Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number), and which are the analogue of Carmichael numbers for Euler pseudoprimes.

Euler–Jacobi pseudoprimes

# Euler–Jacobi pseudoprimes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=10)] Main article: [Euler–Jacobi pseudoprime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Jacobi_pseudoprime)

Another approach is to use more refined notions of pseudoprimality, e.g. [strong pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime) or [Euler–Jacobi pseudoprimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Jacobi_pseudoprime), for which there are no analogues of [Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number). This leads to [probabilistic algorithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_algorithm) such as the [Solovay–Strassen primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solovay%E2%80%93Strassen_primality_test), the [Baillie–PSW primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie%E2%80%93PSW_primality_test), and the [Miller–Rabin primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test), which produce what are known as [industrial-grade primes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial-grade_primes). Industrial-grade primes are integers for which primality has not been "certified" (i.e. rigorously proven), but have undergone a test such as the Miller–Rabin test which has nonzero, but arbitrarily low, probability of failure.

Deceptive nonprime

# Deceptive nonprime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=11)]

A **deceptive nonprime** (called **deceptive prime** by Francis and Ray) is a composite numbers *k* that divide the [repunit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit) with length *k*−1[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_pseudoprime#cite_note-13), a composite number is a deceptive nonprime if and only if it is a Fermat pseudoprime to base 10 and not divisible by 3, the deceptive nonprimes are

 91, 259, 451, 481, 703, 1729, 2821, 2981, 3367, 4141, 4187, 5461, 6533, 6541, 6601, 7471, 7777, 8149, 8401, 8911, 10001, 11111, 12403, 13981, 14701, 14911, 15211, 15841, 19201, ... (sequence [A000864](https://oeis.org/A000864) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

A related sequence is **repunit pseudoprime**, defined as a composite number *k* such that the repunit with length *k* is congruent to 1 mod *k*, a composite number is a repunit pseudoprime if and only if it is a weak pseudoprime to base 10 and not divisible by 3, the repunit pseudoprimes are

 10, 55, 91, 259, 370, 385, 451, 481, 505, 703, 715, 1045, 1105, 1729, 2035, 2465, 2821, 2981, 3367, 4141, 4187, 5005, 5461, 6533, 6541, 6565, 6601, 7471, 7777, 8149, 8401, 8695, 8905, 8911, ... (sequence [A303608](https://oeis.org/A303608) in the [OEIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-Line_Encyclopedia_of_Integer_Sequences))

Applications

# Applications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fermat_pseudoprime&action=edit&section=12)]

The rarity of such pseudoprimes has important practical implications. For example, [public-key cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptography) algorithms such as [RSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(algorithm)) require the ability to quickly find large primes. The usual algorithm to generate prime numbers is to generate random odd numbers and [test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primality_test) them for primality. However, [deterministic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deterministic_algorithm) primality tests are slow. If the user is willing to tolerate an arbitrarily small chance that the number found is not a prime number but a pseudoprime, it is possible to use the much faster and simpler [Fermat primality test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_primality_test).
